title: I'm 55 with a high income. Should I keep buying rental properties?
excerpt: A 55-year-old earning RM32,000 a month wants a third and fourth rental property to pass on. Sean says judge each by yield, and use cash to buy subsale at the right price.

question.asker: From S, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: S turns 55 this year, earns about RM32,000 a month gross and plans to work until 60. She owns a fully paid double-storey corner house worth about RM3 million, has about RM1.7 million in EPF and has just bought a RM1.2 million freehold condo for her own use with a 90% loan, about RM1 million over 15 years at 3.85%. She avoids shares and unit trusts, and wants to grow wealth to pass on to her two sons.
question.text: Is it a good move to buy a third property for rent in Kuala Lumpur, and could she take a loan for a fourth in 2026?

answer.quote: The criteria of investment should be yield.
answer.summary: Yes, both are doable at her income, but a 15-year loan means rent will rarely cover the instalment. Judge each unit by its yield, look at subsale, auction and bulk purchases rather than buying from the developer, and put enough cash down that the rent covers the instalment.

reasons.title: Age shortens the loan
reasons.body: Most banks lend until 65 and some until 70, so she gets about 15 years, not 35. A RM900,000 loan at 4% costs about RM3,985 a month over 35 years but about RM6,657 over 15, which needs roughly RM21,000 of income instead of RM12,000.

reasons.title: Yield is the measure
reasons.body: Divide 12 months' rent by the price; it should be at least 1% above the loan rate to cover interest and maintenance. Sean regards 5% to 6% as normal and 7% as a bonus; 10% to 12% usually means risky short-stay units in tourist areas, which many buildings now ban.

reasons.title: Cash lets her buy with certainty
reasons.body: A third loan is capped at 70%, so a RM1 million unit needs about RM300,000 upfront, or RM350,000 to RM360,000 with renovation. With that cash, a subsale lets her see the unit, its rent and condition, and negotiate.

reasons.title: Compare the whole area, not one project
reasons.body: Around Sunway Velocity and the TRX area, look at the median prices and yields of neighbouring condos as well, and at bulk purchase deals, where buyers can pay less upfront for a better price.

actions: Work out each shortlisted unit's yield and drop anything below about 5%.
Decide how much cash you'll put down so the rent covers the 15-year instalment, and keep enough back for medical bills, family and emergencies.
Compare subsale, auction and bulk purchase prices in the same area before considering a developer's price.
Be wary of deals that look too good to be true, including short-stay units promising very high returns.
Involve your sons now so they understand the properties they will inherit.
caveat: Sean couldn't say whether she should spend, invest or keep her cash; that balance between enjoying it, protection and legacy is hers. Younger buyers can take 35-year loans, so the rent-covers-instalment test suits them better than it does her.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #235. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in January 2024. Sean mentions The Makeover Guys, a renovation company he works with, and bulk purchase clubs in general.
